prime.problem: Counting tests says nothing about whether they would notice a bug. To shrink 764 tests safely you need a measure of what each test actually detects, or you'll throw away the one test that catches something.
prime.fits: HumanEval's 9.6 tests were counted, not weighed. This card gives each test a weight: the seeded bugs it kills. The next card, test-suite reduction, uses those kill sets as requirements.
expect: a mutant = one small injected bug
killing = passes on original, fails on mutant
prime.goal: Build a kill matrix by hand, compute a mutation score, spot a test that carries no information, and explain why some mutants can never be killed.

attend: What exactly has to happen on one input for a test to count as killing a mutant?
Why does n = 1 kill nothing in the worked example, even though it is a sensible edge case?
Which question does mutant killing answer that "did this line run?" can't?
In table 4, where does the killed-mutants column land between coverage and sample killing, and why keep it anyway?
What makes a mutant equivalent, and what does that do to the maximum score?

must: Inject one small bug per mutant (< → <=) → run each test on original and mutant → a different result means the test detects that kind of fault → its kill set measures detection, not execution
Each test's kill set becomes a requirement set → reduction must keep some test for every killed mutant → tests with empty kill sets (like n = 1) are dropped as carrying no information

Mutants are synthetic, not real model errors → they give a theoretical adequacy floor → but in table 4 they preserve less of the HumanEval+ verdict than real sample kills (GPT-4: 82.9 vs 78.7, full 76.2)
Some mutants behave identically to the original on every input → no test can kill them → the score is capped below 100% and a low score may reflect equivalents, not weak tests
elevated: The score depends on the mutation rules chosen → different operators give different numbers → the paper doesn't state its rule set or tool, so its mutation column isn't reproducible from the text alone
reference: table 4's test counts (11.4 tests for killed mutants)

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3–4 sentences what a mutant is, what killing it means, and how kill sets feed test-suite reduction. Then redraw the 4 × 4 kill matrix for is_prime if you can.
checklist: a mutant is the program with one small deliberate bug
a test kills it if it passes on the original and fails on the mutant
mutation score = killed / total; it measures detection
a test's kill set is its requirement set for reduction; empty sets are dropped
equivalent mutants can't be killed, capping the score

retrieve.q: Explain why mutation testing is a better signal than branch coverage for deciding which tests to keep.
answer: coverage asks whether code ran; mutation asks whether a changed program would be noticed
a test can run a line without checking its effect
so mutant kills track the ability to detect faults

retrieve.q: Walk through why M3 (n % i != 0) survives the n = 4 test but dies on n = 7.
answer: n = 4: i = 2 gives 4 % 2 != 0 false; i = 3 gives true → returns False
the original also returns False for 4, so no difference
n = 7: i = 2 gives 7 % 2 != 0 true → returns False, but 7 is prime → killed

retrieve.q: Table 4 shows killed LLM samples preserve the HumanEval+ verdict better than mutants. Why does the paper still keep mutants as a requirement?
answer: sample killing depends on which models and wrong samples happen to exist
mutants and coverage give guarantees that don't depend on any model
the paper calls them base guarantees for theoretical test adequacy

compare.q: Coverage and mutant killing are the paper's two theoretical requirements. What does each count, which design choice makes mutation stricter, and how does each still fail?
answer: coverage counts branches executed; mutation counts seeded faults detected
mutation requires the output to differ, not just the code to run
coverage fails when a test runs a branch without checking it
mutation fails on equivalent mutants and depends on its operators

compare.q: One mutates inputs to find bugs in samples; the other mutates the program to grade tests. Why does EvalPlus need both, and what would break if you dropped either?
answer: program mutation measures which of those tests matter
no input mutation: too few tests to catch wrong samples
no program mutation: reduction loses a model-independent guarantee

predict.q: Add mutant M5: range(2, n) → range(2, n - 1). Commit before checking: which of the four tests kill it, and could any test at all?
predict.answer: None of T1–T4 kills it, and no input can. For any composite n ≥ 4, its smallest divisor is at most √n, which is below n − 1, so the shortened loop still finds it. For primes the loop finds nothing either way. M5 is an equivalent mutant: it caps the mutation score below 100% however good the tests are.

apply.task: Confirm the prediction by brute force: implement the original is_prime and M5 in Python and compare them for every n from −5 to 1,999. Then write M6, a mutant of your own that no T1–T4 kills but some other n does, and give the killing input. Update the kill matrix and mutation score for T1–T4 with M5 and M6 included.
apply.done: Original and M5 agree on all 2,005 inputs. Your M6 has a named killing input outside {1, 2, 4, 7}, and your new score for T1–T4 is 4/6 (M5 and M6 survive), with a note that M5 can never be killed.
apply.hint: An M6 that fails only on odd composites works: range(2, n) → range(2, n, 2) skips odd divisors, so n = 9 gives True. Check that it still agrees with the original on 1, 2, 4 and 7.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: that M5 survives, or that it can never be killed?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why T1 carries no information despite being a good edge case?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: kill set → requirement set, or requirement set → which tests survive reduction?
Could you explain why a lower mutation score doesn't always mean weaker tests?
What will you look for in the test-suite-reduction card: how ties are broken when two tests add the same number?
